name: Question 13
problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}+32y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,x>0.
$$
worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+2x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+32{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+2\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+32{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+2\lambda +32] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+2\lambda +32 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+32 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$  

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
y(x)=A{x}^{4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-4\text{i}}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{4\text{i}}}={e}^{4\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ {x}^{-4\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-4\text{i}}}={e}^{-4\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-4\text{i}} \\  & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & ={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

Question 13
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem

2x2y″+2xy′+32y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=cos⁡(2ln⁡x)+sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
b
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)
c
y(x)=−3sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−2sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=−3cos⁡(2ln⁡x)−sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

2x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+2x⋅λxλ−1+32xλ=02λ(λ−1)xλ+2λxλ+32xλ=0xλ[2λ(λ−1)+2λ+32]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

2λ(λ−1)+2λ+32=02λ2+32=0λ2=−16.

Hence, the roots are λ=±4i.

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(x)=Ax4i+Bx−4i.

Now, we note that

x4i=eln⁡x4i=e4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x)x−4i=eln⁡x−4i=e−4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x).

Therefore,

y(x)=Ax4i+Bx−4i=A(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x))+B(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x))=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x),

where we have set c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=1 into the general solution gives

1=c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=0. First, we differentiate y to find y′:

y′=4x−1(c2cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−c1sin⁡(4ln⁡x))

Substituting y′(1)=0 and c1=1 into the above gives

0=4c2c2=0.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x).
